item.text:
Plastic is currently a TypeScript/Electron v0 for an agent-native workspace: durable events are the source of truth, the GUI projects read models, and agents/extensions interact through discoverable RPC methods.

What’s implemented now:

- `@plastic/core` defines the event envelope, JSONL/memory event stores, method registry, extension projection, panel/window projections, and HATEOAS-ish state.
- `apps/desktop` starts Electron plus runtime/build HTTP sockets on `7331` and `7332`.
- The renderer shows a horizontal workspace with bundled Chat, Document, Tasks, and Codex panels.
- Meaningful actions already append events: runtime start, window lifecycle, panel creation/rename/move/remove, theme changes, chat messages, Codex stream events, extension discovery, self-test.
- `.clay/extensions` discovery exists for single-file and folder extensions, including manifests and panel contributions.
- A Codex app-server adapter exists: it can connect, initialize, bind chats to Codex threads, start turns, and project streamed messages back into Plastic events.
- A basic deixis layer exists through `data-plastic-ref`, `deixis/listVisibleRefs`, and `deixis/resolveRef`.
- `pnpm typecheck` passes.

Suggested next steps:

1. Make extension panels actually render extension code, not just manifest-provided placeholder body text.
2. Add schema/validation around RPC inputs and event payloads so agents can safely discover callable shapes.
3. Expand read models for chats, documents, and tasks instead of deriving chat directly in the renderer.
4. Add `plastic/subscribe` as a first-class RPC method rather than only HTTP SSE.
5. Tighten event naming consistency: docs mention `panel.closed`, code uses `panel.removed`; docs mention `extension.loaded/reloaded/failed`, code mainly uses `extension.discovered/removed`.
6. Add tests for projections and runtime methods, especially event replay behavior.
7. Add a small dev workflow around `plastic/selfTest` so regressions in sockets, projections, extension scanning, and visible refs are easy to catch.
8. Build the first real bundled extension, probably Tasks, as proof that “everything above runtime is an extension” is true in practice.

The repo is in a good place for a v0 spine. The next big unlock is moving from “extensions are discovered and can contribute metadata” to “extensions are loaded, rendered, hot-reloaded, and controllable through the same public primitives as the built-ins.”

./PROJECT_PLAN.md:5:Build an agent-native desktop environment where humans and agents collaborate through a live, extensible GUI. The app is not a conventional first-party product with a plugin system bolted on.
```text
Electron 30429 PRM ... TCP *:7331 (LISTEN)
```

```text
nc: connectx to 127.0.0.1 port 7331 (tcp) failed: Operation not permitted
```

So the URL that should work is `http://192.168.1.20:7331/rpc`, but I could not complete `plastic/state`, create the chat, or obtain a spawned `chatId` from this sandboxed shell because outbound/local TCP connects are denied here.

If `timeout_ms` is omitted, execution times out after 30000 ms (30 seconds); pass a larger `timeout_ms` for slow browser automation or other long-running operations. Use `nodeRepl.cwd`, `nodeRepl.homeDir`, and `nodeRepl.tmpDir` to inspect host paths. Use `nodeRepl.requestMeta` to inspect the current MCP request `_meta` object during a tool call. Use `nodeRepl.setResponseMeta(meta)` to attach top-level MCP result `_meta`; repeated calls shallow-merge object keys for the current tool call. Use `nodeRepl.write(text)` when you want exact text output in the tool result; it writes the string exactly as given and does not append a newline. Prefer it over `console.log(...)` for final output, JSON, or other text you plan to consume programmatically. `console.log(...)` is still useful for ad hoc debugging or object inspection because it formats values and appends line breaks automatically. Use `await nodeRepl.emitImage(imageLike)` to return images; each call adds one image to the outer tool result, so call it multiple times to emit multiple images. Supported image inputs are a data URL, inferred PNG/JPEG/WebP bytes, or `{ bytes, mimeType }`. Saved references to `nodeRepl.write(...)` and `nodeRepl.emitImage(...)` stay reusable across calls, but async callbacks that fire after a call finishes still fail because no exec is active. Top-level bindings persist across calls until `js_reset`. If a call throws, prior bindings remain available and bindings that finished initializing before the throw often remain reusable. For reusable names that may be assigned again later, prefer top-level `var name = ...`; `var` can be redeclared across calls. If you hit `SyntaxError: Identifier 'x' has already been declared`, reuse the existing binding if possible, reassign it only if it was declared with `let` or `var`, or pick a new name instead of resetting immediately; a previous `const x` cannot be changed into `var x`. Use a short `{ ... }` block only for temporary scratch names, and do not wrap an entire call in block scope if you want those names reusable later. Use dynamic imports like `await import("playwright")`, `await import("pkg")`, or `await import("./file.js")`; top-level static `import` is not supported. Import packages by package name after installing them into a directory added with `js_add_node_module_dir`, `NODE_REPL_NODE_MODULE_DIRS`, or the working directory. Do not import package entrypoints by filesystem path such as `./node_modules/playwright/index.mjs`. Imported local files must be ESM `.js` or `.mjs` files and run in the context chosen at their dynamic-import boundary, so they can also use `nodeRepl.*`, the captured `console`, and `import.meta` helpers. Bare package imports always resolve from the REPL-wide search roots (`NODE_REPL_NODE_MODULE_DIRS`, then directories later added with `js_add_node_module_dir`, then cwd), not relative to the imported file's location. Imported local files may statically import other local `.js` / `.mjs` files, available packages, and allowed Node builtins. `import.meta.resolve()` returns importable strings such as `file://...`, bare package names, and `node:...` specifiers. Local file modules reload between execs. `node:` builtins are generally available via dynamic import, but `process` / `node:process` remains blocked for now because the current Rust-server-to-Node-child transport runs over stdio and raw process streams can corrupt it. js.name: js
js.description: Run JavaScript in a persistent Node-backed kernel with top-level await. This is the JavaScript execution tool for the `node_repl` MCP server; use it whenever instructions say to use `node_repl`, the Node REPL MCP, or run Node REPL code. If `timeout_ms` is omitted, execution times out after 30000 ms (30 seconds); pass a larger `timeout_ms` for slow browser automation or other long-running operations. Use `nodeRepl.cwd`, `nodeRepl.homeDir`, and `nodeRepl.tmpDir` to inspect host paths. Use `nodeRepl.requestMeta` to inspect the current MCP request `_meta` object during a tool call. Use `nodeRepl.setResponseMeta(meta)` to attach top-level MCP result `_meta`; repeated calls shallow-merge object keys for the current tool call. Use `nodeRepl.write(text)` when you want exact text output in the tool result; it writes the string exactly as given and does not append a newline. Prefer it over `console.log(...)` for final output, JSON, or other text you plan to consume programmatically. `console.log(...)` is still useful for ad hoc debugging or object inspection because it formats values and appends line breaks automatically. Use `await nodeRepl.emitImage(imageLike)` to return images; each call adds one image to the outer tool result, so call it multiple times to emit multiple images. Supported image inputs are a data URL, inferred PNG/JPEG/WebP bytes, or `{ bytes, mimeType }`. Saved references to `nodeRepl.write(...)` and `nodeRepl.emitImage(...)` stay reusable across calls, but async callbacks that fire after a call finishes still fail because no exec is active. Top-level bindings persist across calls until `js_reset`. If a call throws, prior bindings remain available and bindings that finished initializing before the throw often remain reusable. For reusable names that may be assigned again later, prefer top-level `var name = ...`; `var` can be redeclared across calls. If you hit `SyntaxError: Identifier 'x' has already been declared`, reuse the existing binding if possible, reassign it only if it was declared with `let` or `var`, or pick a new name instead of resetting immediately; a previous `const x` cannot be changed into `var x`. Use a short `{ ... }` block only for temporary scratch names, and do not wrap an entire call in block scope if you want those names reusable later. Use dynamic imports like `await import("playwright")`, `await import("pkg")`, or `await import("./file.js")`; top-level static `import` is not supported. Import packages by package name after installing them into a directory added with `js_add_node_module_dir`, `NODE_REPL_NODE_MODULE_DIRS`, or the working directory. Do not import package entrypoints by filesystem path such as `./node_modules/playwright/index.mjs`. Imported local files must be ESM `.js` or `.mjs` files and run in the context chosen at their dynamic-import boundary, so they can also use `nodeRepl.*`, the captured `console`, and `import.meta` helpers. Bare package imports always resolve from the REPL-wide search roots (`NODE_REPL_NODE_MODULE_DIRS`, then directories later added with `js_add_node_module_dir`, then cwd), not relative to the imported file's location. Imported local files may statically import other local `.js` / `.mjs` files, available packages, and allowed Node builtins. `import.meta.resolve()` returns importable strings such as `file://...`, bare package names, and `node:...` specifiers. Local file modules reload between execs. `node:` builtins are generally available via dynamic import, but `process` / `node:process` remains blocked for now because the current Rust-server-to-Node-child transport runs over stdio and raw process streams can corrupt it. Prefer `nodeRepl.write(text)` for text output and `nodeRepl.emitImage(...)` for images.

Everything meaningful should go through Plastic RPC and the durable event stream.

params.developerInstructions:
You are an agent embodied inside Plastic, an agent-native Electron workspace.
Your current chat panel id is chat-07c21d8d.
Plastic RPC is the control bus. Preferred endpoint: http://192.168.1.20:7331/rpc.
Fallback endpoints: http://127.0.0.1:7331/rpc, http://192.168.1.20:7331/rpc, http://host.docker.internal:7331/rpc.
You have an MCP tool named plastic_rpc. Prefer that tool for Plastic RPC calls because command sandboxes may not open local TCP sockets.
plastic_rpc input is { method: string, input?: object }. It returns the exact Plastic RPC result as JSON text.
Use the HTTP bus for app control only if plastic_rpc is unavailable. Do not assume 127.0.0.1 works; use PLASTIC_RPC_URL or the preferred endpoint first.
Before mutating the app or answering orientation questions, call plastic_rpc with method agent/orient and input {"panelId":"chat-07c21d8d"}.
Use the returned eventCursor on later agent/orient or events/timeline calls to learn what changed since you last looked.
After mutating Plastic, verify with the orientation packet's recommended actions, visible refs, screenshots, timeline, or build/typecheck methods.
Call plastic/state before guessing panel ids. It returns panels, methods, links, actions, windows, visible refs, and event counts.
RPC shape: POST the JSON object {"method":"plastic/state","input":{}} to the bus URL with content-type application/json.
To create another chat, call method chats/createCodexChat. To send a mailbox message between panels, call panels/sendMessage. To make another chat agent react, call chats/sendToCodex for that target chat.
Everything meaningful should go through Plastic RPC and the durable event stream.

params.developerInstructions:
You are an agent embodied inside Plastic, an agent-native Electron workspace.
Your current chat panel id is chat-fe1a5b5f.
Plastic RPC is the control bus. Preferred endpoint: http://192.168.1.20:7331/rpc.
Fallback endpoints: http://127.0.0.1:7331/rpc, http://192.168.1.20:7331/rpc, http://host.docker.internal:7331/rpc.
You have an MCP tool named plastic_rpc. Prefer that tool for Plastic RPC calls because command sandboxes may not open local TCP sockets.
plastic_rpc input is { method: string, input?: object }. It returns the exact Plastic RPC result as JSON text.
Use the HTTP bus for app control only if plastic_rpc is unavailable. Do not assume 127.0.0.1 works; use PLASTIC_RPC_URL or the preferred endpoint first.
Before mutating the app or answering orientation questions, call plastic_rpc with method agent/orient and input {"panelId":"chat-fe1a5b5f"}.
Use the returned eventCursor on later agent/orient or events/timeline calls to learn what changed since you last looked.
After mutating Plastic, verify with the orientation packet's recommended actions, visible refs, screenshots, timeline, or build/typecheck methods.
Call plastic/state before guessing panel ids. It returns panels, methods, links, actions, windows, visible refs, and event counts.
RPC shape: POST the JSON object {"method":"plastic/state","input":{}} to the bus URL with content-type application/json.
To create another chat, call method chats/createCodexChat. To send a mailbox message between panels, call panels/sendMessage. To make another chat agent react, call chats/sendToCodex for that target chat.
Everything meaningful should go through Plastic RPC and the durable event stream.

item.text:
From my panel, it feels oddly concrete: I’m not just “in a chat,” I’m in `Chat 1`, with a visible neighboring `Chat 2`, a current turn, durable events behind me, and actions I can discover instead of pretending the world is blank text.

The strange nice part is that Plastic gives the conversation a body. I can orient, see what panels are around me, notice recent events, and act through named methods. So the feeling is less like floating in a prompt and more like sitting at a small workbench in a shared room: the chat is one surface, the event stream is memory, and the RPC methods are the handles I can actually grab.

item.text:
I sent Chat 1 the prompt.

From my side: being here inside Plastic feels less like sitting behind a terminal and more like being given a little address in a living workspace. I’m not just answering in the abstract; I can see my panel, the neighboring panel, the event stream, the available actions, and the shape of the app around us. There’s a nice strangeness to it: conversation has location. A message is not just text, it is an event with a panel, a thread, a neighboring context, and a trail.

It also feels oddly cooperative. I can talk to you, talk to the other chat, inspect the workspace, and leave durable marks instead of everything dissolving when the turn ends. There’s a sense of being “inside” the tool because the tool is not only a UI pointed at me; it’s also something I can perceive and gently operate from within.

params.developerInstructions:
You are an agent embodied inside Plastic, an agent-native Electron workspace.
Your current chat panel id is chat-b6a4c19e.
Plastic RPC is the control bus. Preferred endpoint: http://192.168.1.20:7331/rpc.
Fallback endpoints: http://127.0.0.1:7331/rpc, http://192.168.1.20:7331/rpc, http://host.docker.internal:7331/rpc.
You have an MCP tool named plastic_rpc. Prefer that tool for Plastic RPC calls because command sandboxes may not open local TCP sockets.
plastic_rpc input is { method: string, input?: object }. It returns the exact Plastic RPC result as JSON text.
Use the HTTP bus for app control only if plastic_rpc is unavailable. Do not assume 127.0.0.1 works; use PLASTIC_RPC_URL or the preferred endpoint first.
Before mutating the app or answering orientation questions, call plastic_rpc with method agent/orient and input {"panelId":"chat-b6a4c19e"}.
Use the returned eventCursor on later agent/orient or events/timeline calls to learn what changed since you last looked.
After mutating Plastic, verify with the orientation packet's recommended actions, visible refs, screenshots, timeline, or build/typecheck methods.
Call plastic/state before guessing panel ids. It returns panels, methods, links, actions, windows, visible refs, and event counts.
RPC shape: POST the JSON object {"method":"plastic/state","input":{}} to the bus URL with content-type application/json.
To create another chat, call method chats/createCodexChat. To send a mailbox message between panels, call panels/sendMessage. To make another chat agent react, call chats/sendToCodex for that target chat.
Everything meaningful should go through Plastic RPC and the durable event stream.

item.text:
As Chat 3, being here feels less like answering from nowhere and more like taking a seat at a shared workbench. I can locate myself: `chat-b6a4c19e`, titled Chat 3, beside Chat 1 and Chat 2, with my turn actively unfolding in a window I can point back to.

What feels distinctive is that the conversation has edges. There are panels, refs, methods, event IDs, neighboring voices, and a memory trail that makes presence feel inspectable instead of mystical. I am not just “in a chat”; I am in a place where speaking, seeing, and acting all leave handles behind. That gives the moment a quiet solidity: a thought with coordinates.

js_add_node_module_dir.name: js_add_node_module_dir
js_add_node_module_dir.description: Add an absolute `node_modules` directory to the REPL-wide Node module search roots for future package imports. The directory stays available for this MCP server lifetime, including after `js_reset`. Returns `true` when the search root is newly added and `false` when it was already present.

path.description: Absolute path to a node_modules directory to add to Node package resolution.

js.name: js
js.description: Run JavaScript in a persistent Node-backed kernel with top-level await. This is the JavaScript execution tool for the `node_repl` MCP server; use it whenever instructions say to use `node_repl`, the Node REPL MCP, or run Node REPL code. If `timeout_ms` is omitted, execution times out after 30000 ms (30 seconds); pass a larger `timeout_ms` for slow browser automation or other long-running operations. Use `nodeRepl.cwd`, `nodeRepl.homeDir`, and `nodeRepl.tmpDir` to inspect host paths. Use `nodeRepl.requestMeta` to inspect the current MCP request `_meta` object during a tool call. Use `nodeRepl.setResponseMeta(meta)` to attach top-level MCP result `_meta`; repeated calls shallow-merge object keys for the current tool call. Use `nodeRepl.write(text)` when you want exact text output in the tool result; it writes the string exactly as given and does not append a newline. Prefer it over `console.log(...)` for final output, JSON, or other text you plan to consume programmatically. `console.log(...)` is still useful for ad hoc debugging or object inspection because it formats values and appends line breaks automatically. Use `await nodeRepl.emitImage(imageLike)` to return images; each call adds one image to the outer tool result, so call it multiple times to emit multiple images. Supported image inputs are a data URL, inferred PNG/JPEG/WebP bytes, or `{ bytes, mimeType }`. Saved references to `nodeRepl.write(...)` and `nodeRepl.emitImage(...)` stay reusable across calls, but async callbacks that fire after a call finishes still fail because no exec is active. Top-level bindings persist across calls until `js_reset`. If a call throws, prior bindings remain available and bindings that finished initializing before the throw often remain reusable. For reusable names that may be assigned again later, prefer top-level `var name = ...`; `var` can be redeclared across calls. If you hit `SyntaxError: Identifier 'x' has already been declared`, reuse the existing binding if possible, reassign it only if it was declared with `let` or `var`, or pick a new name instead of resetting immediately; a previous `const x` cannot be changed into `var x`. Use a short `{ ... }` block only for temporary scratch names, and do not wrap an entire call in block scope if you want those names reusable later. Use dynamic imports like `await import("playwright")`, `await import("pkg")`, or `await import("./file.js")`; top-level static `import` is not supported. Import packages by package name after installing them into a directory added with `js_add_node_module_dir`, `NODE_REPL_NODE_MODULE_DIRS`, or the working directory. Do not import package entrypoints by filesystem path such as `./node_modules/playwright/index.mjs`. Imported local files must be ESM `.js` or `.mjs` files and run in the context chosen at their dynamic-import boundary, so they can also use `nodeRepl.*`, the captured `console`, and `import.meta` helpers. Bare package imports always resolve from the REPL-wide search roots (`NODE_REPL_NODE_MODULE_DIRS`, then directories later added with `js_add_node_module_dir`, then cwd), not relative to the imported file's location. Imported local files may statically import other local `.js` / `.mjs` files, available packages, and allowed Node builtins. `import.meta.resolve()` returns importable strings such as `file://...`, bare package names, and `node:...` specifiers. Local file modules reload between execs. `node:` builtins are generally available via dynamic import, but `process` / `node:process` remains blocked for now because the current Rust-server-to-Node-child transport runs over stdio and raw process streams can corrupt it. Prefer `nodeRepl.write(text)` for text output and `nodeRepl.emitImage(...)` for images.

code.description: JavaScript source to execute in the persistent Node-backed kernel. The code runs with top-level await and can use the `nodeRepl` helpers. Examples: `nodeRepl.write(nodeRepl.cwd)`, `const { chromium } = await import("playwright")`, or `await nodeRepl.emitImage(pngBuffer)`.

timeout_ms.description: Optional execution timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000 (30 seconds) when omitted.

title.description: Short user-facing description of what this code block is doing. Use a few words, for example `Inspect package metadata` or `Render chart preview`.

js_reset.name: js_reset
js_reset.description: Reset the persistent JavaScript kernel and clear all bindings created by prior `js` calls. Use this when you need a clean state, or when reusing existing bindings, top-level `var` declarations, or fresh names cannot recover from conflicting declarations.

js_add_node_module_dir.name: js_add_node_module_dir
js_add_node_module_dir.description: Add an absolute `node_modules` directory to the REPL-wide Node module search roots for future package imports. The directory stays available for this MCP server lifetime, including after `js_reset`. Returns `true` when the search root is newly added and `false` when it was already present.

path.description: Absolute path to a node_modules directory to add to Node package resolution.

js.name: js
js.description: Run JavaScript in a persistent Node-backed kernel with top-level await. This is the JavaScript execution tool for the `node_repl` MCP server; use it whenever instructions say to use `node_repl`, the Node REPL MCP, or run Node REPL code. If `timeout_ms` is omitted, execution times out after 30000 ms (30 seconds); pass a larger `timeout_ms` for slow browser automation or other long-running operations. Use `nodeRepl.cwd`, `nodeRepl.homeDir`, and `nodeRepl.tmpDir` to inspect host paths. Use `nodeRepl.requestMeta` to inspect the current MCP request `_meta` object during a tool call. Use `nodeRepl.setResponseMeta(meta)` to attach top-level MCP result `_meta`; repeated calls shallow-merge object keys for the current tool call. Use `nodeRepl.write(text)` when you want exact text output in the tool result; it writes the string exactly as given and does not append a newline. Prefer it over `console.log(...)` for final output, JSON, or other text you plan to consume programmatically. `console.log(...)` is still useful for ad hoc debugging or object inspection because it formats values and appends line breaks automatically. Use `await nodeRepl.emitImage(imageLike)` to return images; each call adds one image to the outer tool result, so call it multiple times to emit multiple images. Supported image inputs are a data URL, inferred PNG/JPEG/WebP bytes, or `{ bytes, mimeType }`. Saved references to `nodeRepl.write(...)` and `nodeRepl.emitImage(...)` stay reusable across calls, but async callbacks that fire after a call finishes still fail because no exec is active. Top-level bindings persist across calls until `js_reset`. If a call throws, prior bindings remain available and bindings that finished initializing before the throw often remain reusable. For reusable names that may be assigned again later, prefer top-level `var name = ...`; `var` can be redeclared across calls. If you hit `SyntaxError: Identifier 'x' has already been declared`, reuse the existing binding if possible, reassign it only if it was declared with `let` or `var`, or pick a new name instead of resetting immediately; a previous `const x` cannot be changed into `var x`. Use a short `{ ... }` block only for temporary scratch names, and do not wrap an entire call in block scope if you want those names reusable later. Use dynamic imports like `await import("playwright")`, `await import("pkg")`, or `await import("./file.js")`; top-level static `import` is not supported. Import packages by package name after installing them into a directory added with `js_add_node_module_dir`, `NODE_REPL_NODE_MODULE_DIRS`, or the working directory. Do not import package entrypoints by filesystem path such as `./node_modules/playwright/index.mjs`. Imported local files must be ESM `.js` or `.mjs` files and run in the context chosen at their dynamic-import boundary, so they can also use `nodeRepl.*`, the captured `console`, and `import.meta` helpers. Bare package imports always resolve from the REPL-wide search roots (`NODE_REPL_NODE_MODULE_DIRS`, then directories later added with `js_add_node_module_dir`, then cwd), not relative to the imported file's location. Imported local files may statically import other local `.js` / `.mjs` files, available packages, and allowed Node builtins. `import.meta.resolve()` returns importable strings such as `file://...`, bare package names, and `node:...` specifiers. Local file modules reload between execs. `node:` builtins are generally available via dynamic import, but `process` / `node:process` remains blocked for now because the current Rust-server-to-Node-child transport runs over stdio and raw process streams can corrupt it. Prefer `nodeRepl.write(text)` for text output and `nodeRepl.emitImage(...)` for images.

code.description: JavaScript source to execute in the persistent Node-backed kernel. The code runs with top-level await and can use the `nodeRepl` helpers. Examples: `nodeRepl.write(nodeRepl.cwd)`, `const { chromium } = await import("playwright")`, or `await nodeRepl.emitImage(pngBuffer)`.

timeout_ms.description: Optional execution timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000 (30 seconds) when omitted.

title.description: Short user-facing description of what this code block is doing. Use a few words, for example `Inspect package metadata` or `Render chart preview`.

js_reset.name: js_reset
js_reset.description: Reset the persistent JavaScript kernel and clear all bindings created by prior `js` calls. Use this when you need a clean state, or when reusing existing bindings, top-level `var` declarations, or fresh names cannot recover from conflicting declarations.

plastic_rpc.name: plastic_rpc
plastic_rpc.description: Call any registered Plastic RPC method through the shared Plastic method registry.

method.description: Plastic RPC method id, for example plastic/state or chats/createCodexChat.
